docs/adr/0001-one-owner-for-the-tool-grant.md, Consequences: "a mid-call handoff changes the card and must change the grant with it", restated at backend/agent_core/tools/grant.py:15-18. backend/voice/bot.py:1138-1144 filters the tool registry once at session start and nothing re-runs ToolGrant.for_bundle on handoff, so the handing-off agent's grant survives the transfer — the exact state the ADR says it is a prerequisite for fixing.

docs/adr/0002-cardless-agents-are-denied-every-tool.md: "Fail-open becomes structurally unreachable rather than defended by a fix: there is no branch in which an absent card grants a tool." backend/voice/tools.py:2783-2788 sets allowlist = None when card_for(bot_id) raises KeyError, and backend/agent_core/tools/domain.py:1027 reads None as unrestricted (`if allowlist is not None and target not in allowlist`), so a bot with no first-party card may hand off to anything. backend/agent_core/tools/grant.py:26-28 also still documents a legacy escape hatch ("Callers that still need the legacy ungated fallback ask is_cardless and supply it themselves") that the ADR says was deleted.

themes: The Agent Card is published as a contract and read as a suggestion: of its 65 fields, 22 have no runtime consumer anywhere and three more are actively overridden by a hardcoded table, so an operator can author a retention policy, a supervisor-approval requirement or a mission's definition of success, watch every gate go green, and change nothing (RUNTIME-01, RUNTIME-02, RUNTIME-08).

Every duplicated vocabulary in this slice that was given a cross-language drift test has held and every one that was not has drifted, which makes the drift a decision about testing rather than an accident of duplication (RollbackTrigger's pin held while SANDBOX-06, ORG-05 and ORG-06 did not).

Handoff exists as a defined word in CONTEXT.md, as a gate in the compiler and as a chip on the fleet index, but as a mechanism in none of them: the receiving card is never loaded on either channel, and the voice allowlist enforces four Python constants that no clone can match and no published edit can reach (GRAPH-1, RUNTIME-05, ORG-04).

The publish gates are the only place two tabs ever meet, so every cross-tab consequence is invisible while it is being created and then arrives as a number at the publish button — including counts that report a skipped gate as a pass (TOOLS-2, SKILLS-07, OUTBOUND-13).

Wherever a tab and a runtime disagree about a value the runtime wins silently and the tab keeps rendering the operator's number back to them, so the studio reads as a mirror of intent rather than a view of production (SHIP-01, GUARDRAILS-3, OUTBOUND-01).

The control surface is systematically wider than the behaviour beneath it: sliders offer ranges no channel honours, selects offer modes nothing implements, and toggles offer off-switches the runtime adds straight back (GUARDRAILS-4, TOOLS-6, VOICE-3).

Everything an operator would actually need to change about routing — which card answers the phone, which specialist a hop activates, which intent loads which pack — lives in env vars, JSON files and Python dicts that no screen can author, while the screens that look like they author it are read-only derivations (FLEET-9, SKILLS-12, ORG-07).

Failure is rendered as absence across the entire studio, so an unreachable API and a correct empty state produce identical pixels and the confident wrong answer is always the reassuring one (FLOW-8, EVALS-4, OUTBOUND-06).

The audit trail is the least trustworthy screen in the studio: the chain hashes a payload while the page renders unhashed columns, rollbacks change production without writing an entry at all, and the evidence that would let a reader check any of it is fetched and dropped (CHANGELOG-1, CHANGELOG-3, AUTHZ-9).
